chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
title: Poor distribution of the Andy Razaf album and the label owner
summary: About two hundred albums were pressed and nothing came of it; she likes 'Mound Bayou' and 'Massachusetts'.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: But if you don't mind me going back a little bit. The thing that boggles my mind is that just at the time you retired you made that terrific Andy Razaf's record.
Well that was . . .
It's the most jazz like recording that you had made up till that time, anyway.

Well now you see Leonard Feather, he had access to some of these, I guess to this little company Period Records and they weren't even doing pop music. I mean they were doing classical music. And it started when he got the Kirby Group together, you know, and they called up Flow Down Gently, "Sweet Rhythm" and Re-visited. And so then they published that album. I think that those albums were distributed through membership type of arrangement. They weren't on the market. And then Leonard contacted me a few years later and asked me to do this album, "The Tribute To Andy Razaff". Well, as you know Andy Razoff at that time had had, was paralyzed from his waist down and Leonard thought it would be a good idea to do this tribute to Andy and we did that album. I think it's one of the best things I've done on records too. I really do.
Yeah.
And I was still in good voice.
Absolutely. So what you're saying is, the record wasn't really distributed very aggressively.
No, not at all. I don't

WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
suppose over two hundred of those albums were made up.
Okay, there's the phone.
Okay we're back from that interruption. We were talking about the Andy Razaff album.

Yeah. Nothing much came of that because the owner of the company, I mean, I don't know, he was just not in the business of promoting his records, you know. I forget his name. I don't even think he was American. In fact I think most of the Period Records were distributed abroad. I suppose that we were supposed to promote and give the album ourselves.
Yes, and that coincided with your retirement.
Right.
From touring.
That's right. In fact, I've never done any of those songs on the album in public. None of them. I've never sung any of the songs on the album in public, and they're good tunes.
Sure.
I like "Massachusetts". One I especially like is "Mound Bayou," which Leonard claims

the music for, and Andy wrote the lyrics, a very good tune. I'd like to do it. Maybe I'll put them in my repertoire somewhere along the line, one at a time. You know, strangely enough even though when I say when I'm in a club I can sing as many songs as I want to and if I get an engagement like I work, now I do one night club engagement or maybe two nights, and I go on as many as four times a night and I do as many as six and seven songs a set. But when you sum up the number of tunes I've done over the years there are some things I never get a chance to put in my repertoire. At different times someone will come up to me and say, sing such and such a song and they evidentially had the record years and years ago and I don't even remember having done it, you know. And I certainly don't have the arrangements. It isn't the kind of thing where you can say to the piano player, okay "Ochitona" in the key of F or play "A Brown Bird Singing". If I don't have the music with me it's not easy. So what I've found lately is, I dug up some of the things and made out simple lead sheets so that I can do them. You know, give them to the piano player.
